claims.text: The target material is a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy.
The target alloy is initially in a single-phase solid-solution state.
Adding oxygen interstitials will improve the target alloy's mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing.
Adding nitrogen interstitials will improve the target alloy's mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing.
The applicable oxygen or nitrogen interstitial concentration is 1-3 atomic percent.
An applicable operating or test-temperature range is 700-800°C.
Oxygen or nitrogen addition will form or maintain a stable solid-solution phase.
The intervention will produce a sluggish-diffusion effect.
The intervention will produce severe lattice distortion.
A high-entropy effect contributes to the predicted property improvement.
A cocktail effect contributes to the predicted property improvement.
The intervention will increase the alloy's strength relative to the alloy without added oxygen or nitrogen.
The intervention will increase tensile strength relative to the alloy without added oxygen or nitrogen.
The intervention will increase fracture resistance relative to the alloy without added oxygen or nitrogen.
The intervention will improve oxidation resistance relative to the alloy without added oxygen or nitrogen.
Long-term structural and mechanical stability at service temperatures remains uncertain.
The behavior of oxygen or nitrogen interstitials during high-temperature aging is uncertain.
The appropriate control is the same alloy without oxygen or nitrogen interstitial addition.
The hypothesis is falsified if the interstitial-modified alloy does not outperform the unmodified alloy in elevated-temperature or extreme-environment mechanical testing.
